pages.title: SPHEREx - eoPortal
passages: The mission aims to produce the first all-sky near-infrared spectral survey, exploring the history of galaxy evolution, what happened after the Big Bang, and the origins of water and other prebiotic molecules in planetary systems in our galaxy.
SPHEREx was successfully launched on March 11, 2025.
## Quick facts
| Agency | NASA-JPL, CalTech, Ball Aerospace, Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute |
| Launch date | 11 Mar 2025 |
![](/api/cms/documents/d/eoportal/image7-31)
The spacecraft's attitude control system ensures precise pointing, with an accuracy of 34 arcseconds and 1.4 arcseconds of movement per second.
The spacecraft was built by Ball Aerospace and was launched by SpaceX on a Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 4 East (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base, California.
## Overview

The Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx) is a 27-month satellite mission designed to the early universe and produce the first all-sky near-infrared spectral survey.

The mission is led by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), and developed by the California Institute of Technology (CalTech), Ball Aerospace, and the Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute. 1)
SPHEREx will probe the physical processes that drive cosmic inflation and aim to differentiate between various models of inflation.
The SPHEREx telescope, featuring three mirrors with an effective diameter of 20 cm and a field of view of 11° x 3.5°, is designed as an off-axis, freeform, three-mirror anastigmat.
SPHEREx was launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 4 East (SLC-4E) at the Vandenberg Space Force Base, California on March 11, 2025.
The launch was procured by NASA's Launch Services Program and was conducted as a shared mission with the Polarimeter to UNify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) spacecraft.
Since its launch, ground controllers have established communications with the satellite.
The PUNCH satellite successfully separated from the spacecraft approximately an hour after launch, quickly followed by SPHEREx.
On March 18, 2025, SPHEREx ejected the dust cover from its telescope and effectively “opened its eyes” to the universe.
* March 18, 2025: SPHEREx ejected the dust cover from its telescope. 10)

* March 11, 2025: SPHEREx was successfully launched from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California at 8.10 p.m. PDT. Ground controllers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California established communications with the space observatory at 9:31 p.m PDT. 11)

* February 2025: SPHEREx is scheduled for launch, following completion of its integration and testing phases. Once in orbit, the telescope will carry out four complete sky surveys over 25 months, gathering near-infrared spectral data from 450 million galaxies and 100 million stars. 12)

* August 03, 2022: NASA confirmed that SPHEREx will launch alongside the PUNCH (Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere) mission as a secondary rideshare payload. This decision optimizes launch costs and aligns with mission requirements. 13)

* February 04, 2021: NASA awards SpaceX a $98.8 million contract to launch SPHEREx aboard a Falcon 9 rocket. The contract covers launch services, including integration and mission support, with a planned launch from Vandenberg Space Force Base.9)
To maximize data downlink opportunities, it will communicate with ground stations in Troll, Antarctica; Fairbanks, Alaska; Punta Arenas, Chile; and Svalbard, Norway.
These stations are part of NASA’s Near Space Network, managed by NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center.
SPHEREx will have approximately five ground station passes per day, during which the Ka-band will transmit data for about three minutes, while the S-band will be used for about ten minutes.

Scientific data processing and analysis will be handled by the SPHEREx Science Data Center at CalTech’s IPAC, with data releases and archiving conducted through the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). 16)
SPHEREx utilizes S-band and Ka-band frequencies for its communication needs.

passages: # PUNCH Spacecraft Beauty Passes
* **Released** Tuesday, December 5, 2023
* + Visualizations by:

NASA’s Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) mission is a constellation of four small satellites in Sun-synchronous, low Earth orbit that will make global, 3D observations of the young solar wind, from the outermost solar atmosphere to the inner heliopshere.
Images of unprecedented quality will help to close a 60-year gap in measurements of understanding of what occurs in this region of space.
PUNCH will share a ride to space with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory’s Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Re-ionization, and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx) mission.
The missions launched on March 11, 2025, on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 4 East at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.
Get the latest updates on [NASA's PUNCH blog](https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/punch/).
* ###### Movies
* ###### Images
**Conceptual Animation**
A conceptual animation of the PUNCH spacecraft.

Working together, the four suitcase-sized satellites will create a combined field of view and map the region where the Sun’s corona, or outer atmosphere, transitions to the solar wind (the constant outflow of material from the Sun),
**Conceptual Animation**

This conceptual animation shows PUNCH’s four suitcase-sized spacecraft spreading out along the planet’s day-night boundary after being launched into Earth orbit, giving the mission a continuous, unobstructed view of the Sun and its surroundings.
The goal of the animation is to demonstrate how each spacecraft is spaced relative to each other.

## [SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer)](https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/spherex/)
# NASA, SpaceX Update Launch Date for SPHEREx, PUNCH Mission

Technicians and engineers encapsulate NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) observatory and PUNCH (Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere) satellites within a protective payload fairing inside the Astrotech Space Operations facility at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, on Thursday, Feb. 27, 2025.
BAE Systems/Benjamin Fry
NASA and SpaceX now are targeting no earlier than Tuesday, March 4, for the launch of the agency’s SPHEREx and PUNCH missions.
The teams need additional time to evaluate launch vehicle hardware data.
The launch window opens at 10:09 p.m.
EST (7:09 p.m.
PST) from Space Launch Complex 4 East (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.

The [SPHEREx](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/spherex/) mission (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) will improve our understanding of what happened in the first second after the big bang and search for key ingredients for life in our galaxy.
The [PUNCH](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/punch/) mission (Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere) will observe the Sun’s corona as it transitions into the solar wind.
The prelaunch news briefing now is scheduled for 3:30 p.m. on March 3, with coverage streaming live on [NASA+](https://plus.nasa.gov/scheduled-video/spherex-and-punch-pre-launch-news-conference/).
Media may ask questions in person and via phone.
Limited auditorium space will be available for in-person participation.
For the dial-in number and passcode, media should contact the Kennedy newsroom no later than one hour before the start of the event at [ksc-newsroom@mail.nasa.gov](mailto:ksc-newsroom@mail.nasa.gov).
The SPHEREx and PUNCH live launch broadcast will begin at 9:15 p.m., March 4, and stream live [NASA+](https://plus.nasa.gov/scheduled-video/spherex-and-punch-launch/).
Visit the NASA website for more information about [SPHEREx](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/spherex/) and [PUNCH](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/punch/).

passages: # NASA’s SPHEREX and PUNCH Missions Launch from Vandenberg Space Force Base
* **Released** Monday, March 17, 2025
Ignition, and liftoff!
EDT (8:10 p.m.

PDT) March 11, 2025, SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket blasted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base’s Space Launch Complex 4 East, carrying NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) and PUNCH (Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere) missions.
SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) will orbit Earth for a two-year prime mission and create a three-dimensional map of the cosmos.

This will help scientists answer major questions about what happened in the first second after the big bang, how galaxies form and evolve, and the origins and abundance of water and other key ingredients for life in our galaxy.
Ride-sharing with SPHEREx was NASA’s PUNCH (Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere) mission, which will study the outer portion of the Sun, the corona, to understand how solar wind forms.
For more information on SPHEREx: [nasa.gov/spherex](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/spherex/)
For more information on PUNCH: [science.nasa.gov/mission/punch](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/punch/)

**SPHEREx** (**Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ices Explorer**)[[4]](#cite_note-4) is a [near-infrared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared_astronomy "Infrared astronomy") [space observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_observatory "Space observatory") that is performing an [all-sky survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-sky_survey "All-sky survey") to measure the [near-infrared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-infrared "Near-infrared") spectra of approximately 450 million [galaxies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy "Galaxy"). In February 2019, SPHEREx was selected by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") for its next [Medium-Class Explorers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explorers_program#Medium-Class_Explorers_(MIDEX) "Explorers program") mission, beating out two competing mission concepts: *[Arcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcus_(satellite) "Arcus (satellite)")* and [FINESSE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_Infrared_Exoplanet_Spectroscopy_Survey_Explorer "Fast Infrared Exoplanet Spectroscopy Survey Explorer").[[5]](#cite_note-nasa20190213-5)[[6]](#cite_note-Proposals_2017-6) SPHEREx launched on 11 March 2025 on a [Falcon 9 Block 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falcon_9_Block_5 "Falcon 9 Block 5") rocket alongside the [PUNCH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polarimeter_to_Unify_the_Corona_and_Heliosphere "Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere") microsatellites from [Vandenberg Space Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Space_Force_Base "Vandenberg Space Force Base").[[2]](#cite_note-launch-date-2)[[3]](#cite_note-scrubs-3) The principal investigator is James Bock at [California Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Institute_of_Technology "California Institute of Technology") (Caltech) in [Pasadena, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasadena,_California "Pasadena, California").
## Overview
SPHEREx telescope and detectors

The triple mirror telescope has an aperture diameter of 20 centimeters with a 3.5° × 11° field of view and six 2K × 2K [mercury cadmium telluride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_cadmium_telluride "Mercury cadmium telluride") (HgCdTe) [photodetector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photodetector "Photodetector") arrays.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[8]](#cite_note-Sph-inst-8) Each 2K × 2K focal-plane array is covered with a linear variable filter, providing narrow-band response with a band center that varies along one axis of the array.

SPHEREx obtains spectra through multiple exposures, placing a given source at multiple positions in the field of view, where it is measured at multiple wavelengths by repointing the spacecraft.[[8]](#cite_note-Sph-inst-8)
SPHEREx–PUNCH Encapsulation

An enhanced version of SPHEREx was submitted on 15 December 2016 as a [Medium-Class Explorer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explorers_Program "Explorers Program") (MIDEX), and it was selected as a finalist in August 2017, along two other competing missions: *[Arcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcus_(satellite) "Arcus (satellite)")*, and [Fast Infrared Exoplanet Spectroscopy Survey Explorer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_Infrared_Exoplanet_Spectroscopy_Survey_Explorer "Fast Infrared Exoplanet Spectroscopy Survey Explorer") (FINESSE).[[6]](#cite_note-Proposals_2017-6) Each team received US$2 million to refine their mission concepts over nine-months.[[6]](#cite_note-Proposals_2017-6)

SPHEREx was selected as the winner in February 2019, and the mission was approved to proceed with detailed planning.[[5]](#cite_note-nasa20190213-5) On 4 February 2021, NASA announced they had selected the [SpaceX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX "SpaceX") [Falcon 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falcon_9 "Falcon 9") to launch the spacecraft, and total cost of the launch would be US$98.8 million.[[18]](#cite_note-nasa4feb21-18) In August 2022 NASA announced that the 4 microsatellites of the [PUNCH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polarimeter_to_Unify_the_Corona_and_Heliosphere "Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere") constellation would be launched as rideshare payloads together with SPHEREx.[[19]](#cite_note-nasa-20220803-19) The mission launched on 11 March 2025.[[2]](#cite_note-launch-date-2) [First light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_light_(astronomy) "First light (astronomy)") was in April 2025.[[20]](#cite_note-20) Regular science operation started on 1 May 2025.[[21]](#cite_note-21)
The total cost of the mission (design, build, launch, and prime operations) was $488 million.[[1]](#cite_note-press-kit-1)

#### Capturing the Sun’s Influence Like Never Before
*CREDITS: Music: “Crafted with Science Instrumental” by Zak McNeil [ASCAP] via Universal Production Music ; Video: NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center; Producer: Beth Anthony (eMITS)*
![PUNCH mission logo](https://www.thesuntoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/PUNCH_mission_logo.png "PUNCH mission logo")
## PUNCH is Revealing How the Sun Shapes Space

##### PUNCH (Polarimeter to UNify the Corona and Heliosphere) is a groundbreaking NASA mission launched in **March 2025**. It is **tracking how the Sun’s outer atmosphere turns into the solar wind**—a constant stream of charged particles that fills the solar system and affects Earth.
### 🚀 **Stay tuned as PUNCH prepares to unlock the secrets of the solar wind!**
🚀 Launch Date: Tuesday, March 11, 2025
🌍 From **Space Launch Complex 4 East** (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.
🧭 **Orbit:** Low Earth polar orbit along the terminator (day-night) line to maintain a continuous, unobstructed view of the Sun.
🌎 PUNCH is launched with another mission, **[SPHEREx](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/spherex/)**.
## Watching the Solar Wind in Motion
#### ☀️ **Understand the Sun’s Impact on Space**
Instead of looking directly at the Sun, PUNCH will **track how its energy spreads outward**.
![PUNCH Microsatellites](https://www.thesuntoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/PUNCH_Microsatellites-32991-scaled.jpg "PUNCH Microsatellites")
*Image Credit: Courtesy of Southwest Research Institute*
### The Sun’s corona and solar wind are billions of times fainter than the Sun itself, making them extremely difficult to observe.
![PUNCH Data Access and Analysis Tools](https://www.thesuntoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/hp_advance-the-science_400w.gif "PUNCH Data Access and Analysis Tools")
###### PUNCH overcomes this challenge with:
**☀️ Capture large-scale solar structures like never before**
![PUNCH - Polarimeter to UNify the Corona and Heliosphere](https://www.thesuntoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/PUNCH-NFI_LEO.jpg "PUNCH - Polarimeter to UNify the Corona and Heliosphere")
## A Virtual Telescope the Size of Earth

NASA selected Southwest Research Institute to lead a microsatellite mission, PUNCH, which proposes a constellation of four suitcase-sized satellites orbiting Earth to image the Sun’s outer corona and study how its structures connect with the interplanetary medium, better understanding how they infuse the solar wind with mass and energy.
## Following launch, **the four PUNCH satellites will spread out in low-Earth orbit** along the **day-night line**, allowing them to **remain in sunlight with a full view of space**.
“The PUNCH mission will study the solar corona, the Sun’s outer atmosphere, and the solar wind that fills and defines our solar system as a unified, integrated system.
It will provide a crucial missing link in our understanding of the Sun’s influence on the entire solar system.
![SPHEREx Spacecraft on Work Stand in Astrotech](https://www.thesuntoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/PUNCH-KSC-20250117-PH-CAO01_0019.jpg "SPHEREx Spacecraft on Work Stand in Astrotech")
*CREDIT: NASA & USSF 30th Space Wing/Christopher*
![SwRI developed and prototyped the Wide Field Imager for the PUNCH mission.

The dark baffles in the top recess allow the instrument to image objects over a thousand times fainter than the Milky Way.](https://www.thesuntoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/PUNCH-Wide_Field_Imager-32986-440x660.jpg "SwRI developed and prototyped the Wide Field Imager for the PUNCH mission.
The dark baffles in the top recess allow the instrument to image objects over a thousand times fainter than the Milky Way.")
The four spacecraft are launched and deployed in orbit from a single rocket.

Their orbital formation is established over the first 90 days of flight.](https://www.thesuntoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/PUNCH-about_spacecraft.png "Each of the four PUNCH spacecraft is just over a meter long and supports one instrument on the +Z deck (maintained toward the zenith in flight).
Each spacecraft supports three-axis pointing (to within a few arc-seconds), dual-band high-speed downlink, orbital-trim propulsion, and sophisticated, autonomous fault recovery.
Polarization is resolved using a polarizing filter wheel (PFW) assembly, and the image is digitized using a CCD camera assembly (CCA) with a 2kx2k active detector area.

The PFW and CCA designs are common to both instruments.](https://www.thesuntoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/PUNCH-about_NFI-design2_600w.png "The Narrow Field Imager (NFI) is a compact externally occulted coronagraph with a similar field of view to SOHO/LASCO-C3: from 6 to 32 R☉ on the sky.
The external occulter blocks direct sunlight from entering the main optical aperture, which views the corona and starfield around the Sun using a compound lens system.
The U.S. military, private space companies (like SpaceX and Blue Origin), and even financial markets rely on space weather forecasts to prevent major disruptions to critical systems.

## NASA’S PUNCH Mission
## The Sun Touches Humanity
In early 2025, NASA launched a Small Explorer mission called PUNCH, the Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere.
This mission is a constellation of four suit-case sized satellites in low-Earth orbit that make global, 3D observations of the entire inner heliosphere between the Sun and Earth.

quotes.text: The spacecraft was built by Ball Aerospace and was launched by SpaceX on a Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 4 East (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base, California.
The launch was procured by NASA's Launch Services Program and was conducted as a shared mission with the Polarimeter to UNify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) spacecraft.
The missions launched on March 11, 2025, on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 4 East at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.

At 11:10 p.m. EDT (8:10 p.m. PDT) March 11, 2025, SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket blasted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base’s Space Launch Complex 4 East, carrying NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) and PUNCH (Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere) missions.
